paras: The New Orleans knife fight over alleged insolence to a patrolman's wife was a fight in New Orleans, Louisiana, reported on August 31, 1910, between three white men and a group of Black men, after which a Black man lay unconscious and possibly dying. The white men said they had only rebuked the Black men for "insolence" toward the wife of a city patrolman and had been attacked, and the single surviving report gave only their version.

According to a New Orleans dispatch, the trouble began with "insolence displayed by negroes towards a white lady," Mrs. John Meyers, whose husband was a patrolman on the city police force. The dispatch did not describe what the alleged insolence was or where the encounter took place.

Three white men, Tony Grissaffi of Port Street and John and William Schulingkamp of Roman Street, confronted the Black men, by their own account to "admonish" them. In the fight that followed, Grissaffi was wounded in the breast and neck, John Schulingkamp in the right shoulder and arm, and William Schulingkamp, slightly, in the arms and breast. One Black man, who was not named, was "badly beaten and cut" and was unconscious at Charity Hospital, where it was said he might die.

The white men claimed the Black men attacked them, denied that they had been armed, and said they did not cut the Black man and could not account for his injuries. The dispatch did not say who beat him, and it carried no statement from any Black participant or witness.
No report of arrests, of the Black man's recovery or death, or of any court proceeding was found in the coverage.

The only report found ran on the front page of the Hattiesburg News in Mississippi on August 31, 1910, under the headline "Three White Men Are Cut by Blacks." Its subhead called the affair a "row between whites and negroes" resulting from an "alleged insult" to a patrolman's wife, and its opening sentence stated the "insolence" as fact. The story placed the white men's wounds first, although its own text reported that the Black man was the most gravely hurt.
No coverage of the fight was found in the Black press or in New Orleans papers.

accounts.label: White participants' claim
accounts.gist: The three white men said they were not looking for trouble, only admonished the Black men for insolence toward Mrs. Meyers, were attacked, were unarmed, and did not cut the Black man.

framing.detail: The Hattiesburg News headlined the white men as victims ('Three White Men Are Cut by Blacks') and stated the 'insolence displayed by negroes' as the cause, while reporting that the Black man was the most gravely hurt.

sources.note: New Orleans dispatch of Aug. 31: three named white men and an unnamed Black man in Charity Hospital with knife wounds after a row over alleged 'insolence' toward Mrs. John Meyers; only the white men's account is given.
quotes: As the result of insolence displayed by negroes towards a white lady, the wife of Patrolman John Meyers of the police force, three white men and a negro are in the Charity Hospital suffering from knife wounds.
The white men claim they were attacked by the blacks, deny they were armed, and cannot account for the injuries of the negro, whom they assert they did not cut.
The negro was badly beaten and cut, and at the hospital it is said he may die.
The white men state they were not looking for trouble, but only admonished the negroes for their insolence towards Mrs. Meyers.
